# Presenter Script — Parts 2–6

## Slide 4 — FREE WILL IS A MYTH

**[ANIMATION — automatic]** “Free,” then “will,” then “is a myth” appear automatically. Pause until the whole phrase is visible.

“Free will is a myth.”

**[PAUSE — 3 seconds]**

“At least, that’s what we’re going to question today.”

“Think about it. Every decision you’ve made today—from waking up, choosing what to eat, or even participating in our games—you probably believed you made those choices yourself.”

“But what if your brain knows something about your decisions that you don’t?”

“To explore this question, we need to look at one of the strangest discoveries in neuroscience: the split brain.”

**[NEXT SLIDE — press 5]**

## Slide 5 — Two Hemispheres, One Brain

**[ANIMATION — automatic]** The brain image gently floats and the arrow points to the corpus callosum.

“Our brain has two hemispheres: the left and the right. They communicate through a thick bundle of nerve fibers called the corpus callosum.”

“But in some patients with severe epilepsy, doctors have surgically cut this connection to prevent seizures from spreading between the hemispheres.”

“This creates a condition known as the split brain.”

“And here’s where things get interesting. When the two hemispheres can no longer communicate normally, they can sometimes respond to information independently.”

**[NEXT SLIDE — press 5]**

## Slide 6 — The Chicken Claw and Snow Scene

**[ANIMATION — automatic]** The chicken choice appears, then the shovel choice appears.

“In a famous split-brain experiment, researchers showed different pictures to each hemisphere of a patient’s brain.”

“One hemisphere received an image of a chicken claw, while the other received an image of a snowy scene.”

“The patient was then asked to select pictures related to what they had seen.”

“One hand chose a chicken, while the other chose a shovel.”

“That makes sense. A chicken goes with a chicken claw, and a shovel goes with snow.”

“But then researchers asked the patient to explain their choices.”

“The patient explained that the chicken went with the claw, and that the shovel was needed to clean out the chicken shed.”

“The fascinating part? The speaking hemisphere didn’t have access to the snowy scene.”

“Instead of admitting it didn’t know, it created a reasonable explanation.”

“The brain had constructed a story to explain a choice without knowing its actual cause.”

**[NEXT SLIDE — press 5]**

## Slide 7 — Are We Making Choices or Explaining Them?

**[ANIMATION — automatic]** The two thought bubbles pop in around the hand-drawn brain.

“This led neuroscientists to investigate something called the left-brain interpreter.”

“The idea is that parts of our brain try to create a logical explanation for our actions, even when we don’t have all the information.”

“Sometimes, we might genuinely believe we know why we did something, even when our explanation isn’t completely accurate.”

“But does this mean we have no free will?”

“Not necessarily. These experiments don’t prove that free will doesn’t exist. They show that our conscious understanding of our own decisions can be incomplete.”

**[NEXT SLIDE — press 5]**

## Slide 8 — A Question Without a Simple Answer

**[ANIMATION — automatic]** The brain gently thinks on screen.

“Now, I want everyone to think about something.”

“If your brain can make you believe an explanation that isn’t true, how can you be completely certain about why you make your decisions?”

“And if parts of your brain can process information independently, what does that mean for the idea of a single, unified self?”

“So, here’s our final question.”

**[PAUSE — let the class read the question]**

“Do we control our brains, or do our brains control us?”

“Thank you for listening.”
